title: Capstone: a generic statistics library and CLI
body: The capstone combines generic math (stage 7), spans (stage 10), LINQ (stage 9), input validation (stages 1 and 5) and testing. `Stats` provides `Mean`, `Variance`, `Median` and `Histogram` for any numeric type: the input type `T` is constrained to `INumber<T>` and the result type `TResult` to `IFloatingPoint<TResult>`, so integer inputs can produce fractional means.

Algorithms take `ReadOnlySpan<T>` so callers can pass arrays, slices or collection expressions without copying. `Median` copies once into an array to sort, leaving the caller's data untouched, which the API contract promises. `Histogram` uses .NET 9's `CountBy` and returns pairs sorted by value.

The CLI reads one number per line from standard input using invariant culture (so `3.5` parses the same everywhere), reports the first bad line with its line number on standard error and exits with code 1. Formatting uses `FormattableString.Invariant` for the same reason.

Tests use `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]` to cover odd and even counts in one method, and check the population variance against a known textbook data set (mean 5, variance 4). The validator injects an off-by-one bug into `Median` to show the theory catches it.
Run `dotnet test`, then `dotnet run --project src/Statistics.Cli < data.txt` (the validator pipes `data.txt` to standard input).

Practice: add `Percentiles.Percentile<T, TResult>(values, p)` using linear interpolation between closest ranks (p from 0 to 100), with validation, tests that the 50th percentile equals the median, and a `p90` line in the CLI output.
projectInstructions: Run dotnet test, then dotnet run --project src/Statistics.Cli < data.txt. Practice: add a generic Percentile with linear interpolation, tests, and a p90 line in the CLI.

projectChecks.name: start: injected median bug is caught
start: injected sum-in-T overflow is caught

challenge: Add a generic Percentile with linear interpolation, tests that p50 equals the median, and a p90 line in the CLI.
question: Why does Stats use two type parameters, T : INumber<T> and TResult : IFloatingPoint<TResult>?
correct: So integer inputs can produce fractional results such as a mean of 2.5
wrong: Because INumber<T> cannot be used with spans
To make the methods run in parallel
reasoning: Averaging ints in int arithmetic would truncate; converting into a floating-point TResult keeps precision while still accepting any numeric input.
recallAnswer: Constrain inputs to INumber<T> and results to IFloatingPoint<TResult> so integer data yields fractional statistics; accept ReadOnlySpan<T> without copying the caller's data; parse with invariant culture; and cover odd/even and empty cases with theory tests.
